statement: Linear B's signary is derived from Linear A's (visually similar sign forms, shared syllabic sign inventory); Mycenaean scribes repurposed that signary to notate a completely different, known language — Greek — with phonetic modifications for Greek sound patterns. Michael Ventris announced in 1952 that Linear B encoded archaic Mycenaean Greek; John Chadwick independently confirmed it; jointly published in the Journal of Hellenic Studies (1953) and Documents in Mycenaean Greek (Cambridge University Press, 1956, published after Ventris's death). Cracking Linear B did not solve Linear A precisely because sign forms carry over but sign-to-sound values do not transfer across different underlying languages.

sources.citation: Ventris, Michael, and John Chadwick. "Evidence for Greek Dialect in the Mycenaean Archives." Journal of Hellenic Studies, 1953.
